title: Nearby cycles over a trait commute with arbitrary base change
statement:
Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring (a local principal ideal domain of dimension one), let $B=\operatorname{Spec}R$, let $\Lambda$ be a finite commutative ring, and assume $m\Lambda=0$ for an integer $m\geq1$ invertible on $B$. Let $f:T\to B$ be a finite-type morphism [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] and $L\in D^b(T_{\mathrm{Et}},\Lambda)$. Then $(f,L)$ is $\Psi$-good in the sense of [def-trf-oriented-nearby-cycles]: for every scheme morphism $g:B'\to B$, writing $T'=T\times_BB'$, $h:T'\to T$, $f':T'\to B'$ and $v:V_{f'}\to V_f$, the canonical map
$$v^*R\Psi_fL\longrightarrow R\Psi_{f'}h^*L$$
is an isomorphism. No flatness, properness or smoothness of $f$ is required.

source.place: Section 4.5, Example 4.26(2), valuation-ring case, p. 37 of the author PDF; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The ring $R$ is a principal ideal domain, hence Noetherian by the PID lemma. Thus $B=\operatorname{Spec}R$ is locally Noetherian by its one-chart definition and quasi-compact by the affine-scheme lemma; it is integral since $R$ is a domain. Finite type over a Noetherian scheme makes $T$ Noetherian, and the locally-Noetherian quasi-separatedness lemma makes $T$ quasi-separated. In particular $T$ is qcqs. These deductions require neither separatedness nor flatness of $f$. The coefficient ring is Noetherian because it is finite.

source.place: Section 4.5, Example 4.26(2) and Theorem 4.27(1), printed p. 37 (PDF page 37); read online from the author PDF, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: First take a constructible sheaf $F$ of $\Lambda$-modules on $T_{\mathrm{Et}}$, regarded as a complex in degree zero. Apply the modification theorem to $(B,f,F[0],\Lambda,m)$: step 1 supplies its integral Noetherian base, and $F[0]$ is bounded with constructible cohomology. It produces $r:B_1\to B$, proper and an isomorphism over a dense open $U\subset B$, with $(f_1,r_T^*F)$ $\Psi$-good. This is the general-base existence theorem, rather than a trait base-change theorem assumed for $F$.

source.place: Section 4.5, Example 4.26(2) and Theorem 4.27(1), printed p. 37 (PDF page 37); read online from the author PDF, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The generic point $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ belongs to the dense open $U$. Its inverse image under the isomorphism over $U$ gives a $B$-map $\eta\to B_1$. The local PID $R$ is a valuation ring: for nonzero $a,b$, write $(a,b)=(d)$, $a=du$, $b=dv$; then $(u,v)=R$, so one of $u,v$ is a unit in the local ring, and either $a/b$ or $b/a$ belongs to $R$. The proper valuative existence criterion extends $\eta\to B_1$ across $B=\operatorname{Spec}R$ to a $B$-map $s:B\to B_1$. Being a $B$-map says exactly $rs=1_B$. Thus the modification has a section; no completeness, henselianity or excellence of $R$ was used.

source.place: Section 4.5, Example 4.26(2) and Theorem 4.27(1), printed p. 37 (PDF page 37); read online from the author PDF, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Write $\beta_a$ for the ordinary comparison for base change $a$. For successive base changes $a:S_0\to S_1$ and $b:S_2\to S_0$, the definition by the pulled-back counit gives $\beta_{ab}=\beta_b\circ v_b^*\beta_a$, under the canonical pullback identifications: transposing the right hand side gives the counit for $a$ followed by that for $b$, and the middle adjunction unit and counit cancel. Consequently goodness is preserved by base change: if the pair over $S_1$ is good, both $\beta_a$ and $\beta_{ab}$ are isomorphisms for every $b$, so $\beta_b$ is an isomorphism. Apply this to the good pair of step 2 and $a=s$. Since $rs=1_B$, its pullback along $s$ is $(f,F)$ with the specified ordinary comparison. Hence every constructible $F$ on $T$ is good.

source.place: Section 4.5, Example 4.26(2) and Theorem 4.27(1), printed p. 37 (PDF page 37); read online from the author PDF, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For a filtered diagram $(F_i)$ of module sheaves, each functor $R^q\Psi_f$ preserves its colimit. Indeed pull back the natural comparison $\operatorname{colim}_i R^q\Psi_fF_i\to R^q\Psi_f(\operatorname{colim}_iF_i)$ by each strict-local section $\sigma_x$. These inverse images are exact, preserve colimits as left adjoints, and are jointly conservative. The strict-local description identifies this comparison with $\operatorname{colim}_i R^q a_*(F_i|_{T_{(x)}})\to R^q a_*((\operatorname{colim}_iF_i)|_{T_{(x)}})$, for $a:T_{(x)}\to B_{(f(x))}$. Both strict localizations are affine; the morphism-between-affines lemma and affine permanence make $a$ qcqs. Higher direct-image continuity gives precisely the required isomorphism. The same argument applies to $f':T\times_BB'\to B'$ for arbitrary $B'\to B$: it remains locally finite type, and its strict-local schemes remain affine, even when $B'$ is not Noetherian. The torsion condition required by the strict-local description follows from $m\Lambda=0$. All restrictions and inverse images preserve the sheaf colimits by their module adjunctions.

source.place: Section 4.5, Example 4.26(2) and Theorem 4.27(1), printed p. 37 (PDF page 37); read online from the author PDF, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Now let $F$ be any module sheaf on $T$. Since $T$ is qcqs and $\Lambda$ finite, constructible approximation writes $F=\operatorname{colim}_iF_i$ for a small filtered diagram of constructible module sheaves. Fix any $g:B'\to B$. Exact inverse image and step 5 identify $H^q(\beta_{g,F})$ with the colimit of the isomorphisms $H^q(\beta_{g,F_i})$ of step 4, for every $q$: on the source use $v^*R^q\Psi_f$, and on the target use $R^q\Psi_{f'}h^*$. Naturality of the counit defining $\beta$ identifies the map between these two colimits with the one induced by the $\beta_{g,F_i}$. Thus $H^q(\beta_{g,F})$ is invertible for every $q$, which is exactly invertibility in the derived category. This proves goodness for all sheaves without imposing constructibility on $F$.

source.place: Section 4.5, Example 4.26(2) and Theorem 4.27(1), printed p. 37 (PDF page 37); read online from the author PDF, local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Finally choose $a\leq b$ with $H^q(L)=0$ outside $[a,b]$, and fix $g:B'\to B$. The right derived direct images $R\Psi_f,R\Psi_{f'}$ are triangulated, and the exact inverse images are triangulated termwise. The comparison commutes with shifts: use the shifted K-injective resolution $I[1]$ for $K[1]$; its defining adjunct is the shift of the adjunct for $K$, since inverse images, the counit and pullback identifications commute termwise with shifts. Naturality and the shift-compatible-transformation lemma therefore give a morphism of image triangles. Apply both sides to the truncation triangles $\tau_{\leq q-1}L\to\tau_{\leq q}L\to H^q(L)[-q]\to(\tau_{\leq q-1}L)[1]$. Step 6 gives the comparison isomorphism on $H^q(L)[-q]$. Starting from $\tau_{\leq a-1}L=0$, induction for $q=a,\ldots,b$ gives it on $\tau_{\leq q}L$: in the morphism of long exact cohomology sequences, the four adjacent maps are isomorphisms, so the middle map is an isomorphism by the elementary five-lemma argument. As $\tau_{\leq b}L\simeq L$, this proves the displayed comparison for $L$ and every $g$, hence precisely $(f,L)$ is $\Psi$-good.
